records.title: Show HN: Open-source model routing for coding agents at Astra-level performance
records.author: adchurch
records.storyText:
A few months ago we started building a model router for coding agents because we thought we could outperform any single model with an ensemble approach. Recently we’ve achieved that milestone and I want to talk about how we did it.

First of all, a quick explanation: the Weave Router (https://github.com/weave-os/router) plugs into any coding agent (e.g. Claude Code or Codex) and intelligently switches between LLMs. So, for example, Astra handles tricky debugging or complex system design tasks, and Deepseek v4 Flash handles simple frontend updates.

What we’re announcing today is our new routing model, which we’re calling Weave Router 2.0. We benchmarked 2.0 against GPT-6 Astra on Terminal Bench 4.0 and SWE Atlas. On both benchmarks, the router had equivalent pass rates. On Terminal Bench, the router hit 52% of Astra’s cost, and completed tasks 2.2x faster. On SWE Atlas, the router cost 54% as much as Astra and ran 2.5x faster. (Full results on our website at https://weaveos.com/router!)

It turns out training a model to route effectively - taking into consideration model capabilities, costs, cache awareness, and more - is a really hard problem! I want to talk about three ways we were able to improve so much over the last few months: 1) a new architecture, 2) larger training data set size, and 3) smarter cache-eviction impact calculation.

1) a new architecture. Our initial approach used an RL model without many priors. While RL is still an important part of the story, the cost of fully exploring the space of routing decisions is very high, so we’ve taken some shortcuts that have significantly improved performance.

Consider how large the search space for the routing problem is. Take a typical coding agent session, with ~100 agent turns (i.e. 100 LLM API calls). Technically there are 100 chances to select a model. If we assume a roster of ~10 models (of course there are lots more but we can remove any that are Pareto dominated), then there are 10^100 possible paths through that session. We simply cannot explore all of them! So that's why clever tricks to shrink this space are so important.

In particular: we trained a hidden Markov model to trace the session state, then a classifier maps the session to one of a few buckets of similar models. Using the HMM allows us to evaluate not just where a session is currently, but how it got there. We've gotten significantly better performance on bucket selection by incorporating that information - we believe this is because two sessions that might look quite similar to a naive classifier are much better distinguished by this HMM approach.

Using this HMM + classifier to select a bucket first significantly shrinks the space to explore, by throwing out most models that could not reasonably serve the given session. This rearchitecture was the single biggest performance unlock!

2) larger training data set size (much less technically interesting but still an important part of the story). By using frontier LLMs to help us label a larger and more diverse set of coding agent sessions, we were able to bootstrap the two models discussed in 1) to a better state, while also providing even richer reward signals for RL.

3) smarter cache-eviction impact calculation. One of the hardest parts of routing well (if you care about saving money) is using the model caches intelligently. We built a subsystem that can calculate the expected value of switching models (and thus paying a high one-time cost to fill up a different cache) much more accurately, helping us avoid costly and unnecessary switches in more cases, while still switching when the benefit outweighs the cost. This is where most of our improvement on cost has come from.

We still have a lot of room to continue to improve (we won’t rest until we’re consistently beating Astra/Fable, not just tying!) but matching frontier model performance was a huge milestone for our routing model, and in my opinion validates our initial hypothesis that an ensemble of models can do better than any single model ever could.

Our router is open source (https://github.com/weave-os/router) so anyone can try it out. Or if you prefer you can use our hosted version (https://weaveos.com/router).

I started using this a little over half a year ago to help me navigate through some large AI coded PRs people were submitting, because I felt like if I looked at the PR on Github I would just auto pass it through because I didn't want to deal with it. records.title: Show HN: Helo – An email API from former Postmark folks
records.author: Archanian
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Ryan, engineer and co-founder at Helo (https://www.helohq.com) - an email API for sending transactional and marketing email from your application: password resets, receipts, notifications, newsletters, etc.

Most of our team worked together at Postmark for many years, so we know what it takes to build a reliable email service. If you've ever loved a product and then watched it get acquired, you probably know the rest of that story. We started Helo to keep building the kind of product we're good at, improve on what we have learned, take good care of our customers, and stay independent while doing it. We're bootstrapped and plan to stay that way.

Helo covers everything you'd expect from a developer-focused email service:

- REST API and SMTP, with SDKs for Ruby, JS, C#, Python and Go (more to come) - Separate infrastructure for transactional and broadcast mail - Event logs, stats, webhooks, suppressions, unsubscribes, flexible permissions - Usage-based pricing with no arbitrary feature gates - https://www.helohq.com/pricing

Beyond the fundamentals, we've also put a lot of work into multi-tenant sending. When you're a platform sending on behalf of your own customers, you need to keep one bad sender from hurting everyone's deliverability, let customers send from their own domains, and keep stats and unsubscribes separate per customer.

We've built Helo to address all of these concerns, while also allowing flexibility in how the relationships between domains, webhooks, credentials, etc. are defined amongst your tenants. For example, you can share one verified domain across all your customers while letting a few use their own, send all events to one webhook or split them per tenant, and give tenants isolated credentials with permissions limited to exactly what they need.

If you've built multi-tenant sending before, what was most painful? Is there something you wish your email provider handled for you but doesn't? I'd love to hear about it.

records.title: Show HN: Token compression CLI to save Codex/Astra costs
records.author: yolandac
records.storyText:
Hey HN! Yolanda and Spencer here - wanted to share a token compression tool that we’ve built for ourselves to save 30% costs on codex!

After maxing out sub and burning $700/day per person on api, we fine tuned a compression model to trim codex's tool call output to reduce input token + cache. It cut down tokens by 29.6% and now I just leave it on by default in Codex.

To avoid messing up w/ cache, we use proxy + fine tuned qwen model trained on preserving agent trajectory to remove tool call results before they go back to the model, leaving kv cache untouched.

The cli is free for everyone to use (https://github.com/spenmcke/compress). Just lmk ur feedback and hacks to shave even more costs on astra! If you want to integrate it into your product to offer the best models at low cost, I can set you up with an sdk and api keys

PS: It’s built for coding agents, not conversational agents. I optimized it for file retrieval accuracy, trajectory preservation, and quality to get up to 30% cost reduction depending on how context-heavy the task is.

On security and privacy side, it's a proxy wrapping your local codex and ZDR so it doesn't retain any queries. It’s on by default in codex and when you don’t want compression, you can use `codex --uncompress` to disable it.

Give it a try: code is in https://github.com/spenmcke/compress

You can install the cli using

`curl -fsSL https://install.everestagi.com/install.sh | sh && source ~/.config/everest/shell.sh`

Love to hear any feedback and learn your hacky ways to save token costs too!

records.title: Show HN: The Kio Programming Language
records.author: jdevuyst
records.storyText:
Kio is a statically typed, hosted language that is designed to be ultra-portable. Kio 0.1 supports eight host languages and more will be added in the coming weeks.

Kio is based on polymorphic lambda calculus with higher-kinded types. Kio has type-driven macros (elaborators) and it can statically check asserted equivalences using a normalizer.

Kio is a minimalistic language. It doesn't have built-in effectful functions and it doesn't even have built-in string or numeric types. Instead programs declare the capabilities they need and the host supplies them.

The language is designed with AI, which is bound to raise some eyebrows, so I blogged about that here: https://jdevuyst.github.io/kio/blog/2026-10-01-introducing-k...

records.title: Show HN: Silta: family assistant on Matrix with continuity across context limits
records.author: dmitry-markin
records.storyText:
Silta is a self-hosted assistant serving multiple users from a single Matrix account, used by me, family, and close friends for the last three weeks. It runs on Claude Code with each person using their own Claude subscription.

Silta answers everyday questions, conducts web research (presenting the results as PDFs), performs scheduled tasks to monitor/research something and notify you if needed.

It uses a deliberate handoff & compaction procedure, writing the compaction summary itself with a custom prompt, so the thread of the conversation and its picture of the user is preserved across context limits. As it turned out, the assistant accessible in a continuous chat (contrary to ChatGPT / Claude Web sessions) builds up better context about you and your tasks, and provides more relevant answers and help.

It runs on Claude Code as the only allowed way to use a personal Claude subscription. Using Claude Code also spares me developing a harness, at the cost of tracking changes as new versions of Claude Code are released. The assistant itself (the daemon, the channel plugin, the supervisor, and the deployment) is open-source, while the model and the harness are Anthropic's and proprietary.

Silta is deployed to a dedicated VM with separate Linux users per session and systemd hardening, protecting sessions from each other. Claude Code's bubblewrap sandbox is used to protect the Claude credential and the harness's state from the agent. This does not protect from prompt injections coming from search results and potentially leaking user data.

Matrix E2EE protects the conversation from a Matrix server operator, but everything in the context is of course sent to the model provider. Private content is never logged, and the operator is expected to respect the privacy and not read the session transcripts on disk. Additionally, it is recommended to use full-disk encryption and tell the users how their data is handled.

Silta only works in its workspace with files explicitly shared by users in the chat. Giving it access to a user's own computer or services like email is not planned.

Since Opus 5.5 has been released, it is possible to run a session on a $20 Claude Pro subscription. Before that, only Fable 5.1 was pleasant enough to talk to. When run on Anthropic API, a moderately used session extrapolates to $100-$150 per month, with each research run costing $6-$12.

Silta is built with Claude Code and Silta itself. The design, review, deployment, and testing are mine.

records.title: Show HN: Desbordante 2.5.0 Released
records.author: chernishev
records.storyText:
Almost a year has passed since Desbordante’s last release, and now we’re rolling out a new one — 2.5.0.

Desbordante is an open-source, high-performance data profiler that finds and validates complex patterns in data using a bunch of advanced algorithms.

Unlike the black-box ML approaches that dominate today, Desbordante takes a symbolic, explainable approach to data analysis, producing explicit rules or rule-shaped artifacts that are verifiable, such as data dependencies, association rules, or other patterns. It’s a different way to analyze data, and it works well alongside black-box models. Unlike free-form model output, these patterns have precise semantics and can be validated algorithmically against the data. And, importantly, no hallucinations or misclassification.

This release adds 9 new patterns, including support for another dataset type: sequences in data. That brings the total to 4. We also picked up Python 3.15, which just came out. On top of the new patterns, there was a lot of infrastructure work too — mostly invisible to users, but important.

records.title: Show HN: Inbox Cleanup – get to inbox zero in Gmail
records.author: jtiret
records.storyText:
We've been working on a small tool that can help with huge (or really, any size) Gmail inboxes. It's meant for people who have let their inbox grow for years and don't know where to start.

We had this idea after talking to a lot of people about how they use their email, and one thing that kept coming up was how hard it is to keep up when you receive a lot of emails. Things pile up and cleaning up starts to feel impossible.

One important detail: the tool never performs any destructive operations on your email. The most it can do to a message is archive it (move it to the All Mail folder), where it stays available for search, so you never lose any messages as a result.

It combines multiple approaches to inbox cleanup: - You choose a cutoff date to archive everything before that - With some help from OpenAI, we find other groups of emails you may want to archive - We detect newsletters you rarely open and let you unsubscribe in one click - For transactional emails you rarely open (e.g. tool notifications), we suggest filters that skip the inbox and keep them under a label instead

At the end, you can undo all the inbox changes you made.

Gmail API calls happen client-side. Also, your messages and contacts are not stored on our servers. Some message metadata and snippets are sent to OpenAI to help with categorization.

Curious how many of you actually use inbox zero, or have considered trying it?

Happy to get your feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Read the Odyssey in Greek while learning Greek
records.author: ethanedwards
records.storyText:
I made a way to (sort of) read the Odyssey in Greek without all those years of learning Greek first.

I’ve had a deep interest in reading great literature in its original language since I studied Latin in High School, but wanted to find ways of reading real literature quickly. I’ve used this method myself to read books in several languages including Italian, German, Chinese, Japanese, and Greek. You still have to do the grammar and vocabulary study over time to really comprehend it, but this method has worked far better than all my previous attempts. The goal is to eventually be able just to read the language without any aids, but do that while reading real stuff the entire time. I’ve found that I go from needing help on everything, to learning individual words, to phrases, and then gradually I get to understanding whole sentences without looking anything up. Using a translation helps to keep me honest.

records.title: Show HN: Autobox – Make your agents sandbox themselves
records.author: freakynit
records.storyText:
https://github.com/freakynit/autobox

First of all: this is NOT for folks who are already using a sandbox. The guarantees provided by Autobox are weaker. This is rather for folks who "hesitate" to use sandboxes.

Autobox is built around two observations I kept making over past one year of seeing sandbox launches and their real-world usage:

1. There are many sandboxing options now, and they work well. But leaving a handful few, almost nobody uses them. The blocker isn't the technology, it's the setup friction — however small it looks on paper, it's enough that people skip it entirely.

2. LLMs mostly don't write harmful code or take destructive steps. They're not adversarial by default.

Autobox bets on the second observation to remove the first. Instead of asking you to configure a sandbox, it's just there: every tool call carries its own permissions, and anything you don't explicitly allow is denied.

Is it perfect? No - seatbelt filesystem rules are best-effort, and the strong isolation is the V8 path.

Is it better than using no sandbox at all? Definitely yes.

This is also for M-series Macs only.

---

Oh, and the best part: "copy_then_sync":

Using APPFS `clonefile`, Autobox can hand your agent a full, "writable" copy of a repo instantly (1-2 ms). The agent gets something it can freely "destroy", but, your actual working tree is untouched. Your agent can then verify things, and of all looks okay, in one command sync the changes back to host within milliseconds.

Hey HN,

After the visit, it provides a summary including next steps, so you can focus on the conversation instead of taking notes.

The idea of Sidekick came from our team's experiences with healthcare. Our founder, Rahul, had stage three cancer at 17. That's useful and a step in the right direction, but we kept coming back to the fact that a lot of the challenge originates while the conversation is still happening. If you can catch something in the moment, you can address it with your clinician immediately and potentially lead to better outcomes. If you realize you missed something after the visit, then you have to try to get another appointment (and in SF I often can't get another doctor visit till 2 months later).

So we built Sidekick, to help patients and caregivers during a visit in real-time to translate medical jargon and suggest useful questions, ideally without becoming a distraction.

If you want to try it, you can download it on our website. Sidekick is desktop-only for now, but we’re working on a mobile app for in-person visits.

records.storyText:
Business intelligence is changing. AI can now do more than turn a question into a single SQL query: it can investigate a question through a series of queries, examining the result of one query to decide what to query next.

Today, to answer a business question against a database, analysts use a tool like Tableau: they select relevant data, build an initial view using fields, filters, calculations, and visualizations, then look for patterns or anomalies. They form hypotheses and test them — filtering by region, drilling into customer cohorts, comparing time periods, or creating calculations to validate or rule out an explanation. They repeat this process until the evidence supports an answer, then save a workbook or dashboard for others to review and monitor.

With a single question, AI can now perform much of this exploratory loop: it can investigate the data, follow the evidence through multiple queries, and present the supporting analysis. This is agentic data analysis — AI autonomously decides what to investigate next based on the results it has already found.

Reportr puts agentic AI at the center of the experience, then builds complementary capabilities around it to address AI's limitations:

SEMANTIC LAYER

Production databases are rarely clean: columns that are no longer used, cryptic names like status2, misc, or flag, columns whose meaning has quietly shifted over time, tables that linger long after their purpose is gone, and so on. This is known as schema rot. AI tools guess wrong against schemas like this. Reportr's semantic layer lets you give tables and columns business-friendly names and descriptions, document relationships, capture business rules, and flag what AI should ignore — so it's working from what your data means, not just what it's called.

USER OVERSIGHT

AI-generated answers can be wrong. Reportr lets you inspect the SQL executed to arrive at an answer. It also provides explanations of what the SQL does (understandable by business users), and how it works (intended for technical users). You can review the analysis rather than simply accepting AI's conclusions.

BETTER USER EXPERIENCE

Reportr UI is specifically optimized for chatting with a database. Database queries often return large number of records. Ask which customers haven't placed an order in the last 90 days, and the answer is a list of customers. Reportr displays tabular data in an interactive grid that can handle thousand of records without breaking a sweat. The grid supports sorting, searching, and filtering.

REPORTS AND DASHBOARDS

Chat is ephemeral. Every conversation starts fresh, and that's fine for exploration — but not for information you need every week. When a chart or table reveals something worth tracking, save it as a report. Combine reports into dashboards to monitor changes over time, share findings, and keep important insights accessible without having to ask the same questions again.

ROLE BASED ACCESS CONTROL

Not everyone on your team needs the same level of access. Reportr's role-based access control lets you give each user exactly the permissions they need — from view-only access to report building, database management, and full administrative control.

CENTRALIZED MANAGEMENT

Reportr is a web application — there's nothing to install, nothing to update, and no desktop app to manage across your team. Database connection strings, AI keys, are all managed centrally. Reportr can connect to all supported databases directly, MCP servers and drivers are not needed.

INSTALL ON-PREMISE

Reportr can be self-hosted on your own infrastructure, ensuring your data never touches our servers. You can supply your own AI API key. Your data will not be used for training AI models. If you use Claude on AWS Bedrock, Amazon additionally guarantees that your data is never stored or used for training — and Bedrock is HIPAA eligible.

GIVE IT A WHIRL

Visit https://reportr.com to give it a try. We look forward to getting your feedback.

records.storyText:
Hi everyone, we’ve just open-sourced two command-line tools for benchmarking Elasticsearch performance and creating Elasticsearch indexes.

Benchmarker: https://github.com/Vesiro/vesiro-benchmarker Indexer: https://github.com/Vesiro/vesiro-indexer

We’re building a product designed to improve Elasticsearch performance, and needed a consistent way to create test indexes and rerun search workloads after making changes to our setup. You can use vesiro-benchmarker to run repeatable search benchmarks against an existing Elasticsearch index, and vesiro-indexer is designed to create Elasticsearch indexes from Common Crawl data.

For us, reproducibility in our benchmarking is very important. This is why we chose Common Crawl as a data source, as it enables other people to obtain the source data and inspect how we build test indexes. It also doesn’t hurt that there is tons of Common Crawl data, so we can index very large amounts.

Depending on your needs, you might not need both tools. If you already have your own indexes and just need a simple way to start benchmarking, the benchmarker will be enough. If you are only looking for a way to set up test indexes you might be fine just using the indexer.

We are interested to hear how these tools fit the way other teams benchmark Elasticsearch. Feedback on the query workloads or the Common Crawl indexing setup would be particularly helpful.

records.title: Show HN: A 311 byte Klotski solver in C++
records.author: midnight_dream
records.storyText:
Hi all! I made a 311 byte Klotski solver in C++

So back when I first got to use a mobile phone in 2012 I used to play a lot of puzzle games. These were notoriously hard to solve (on high levels), and I always wondered how are these created, how do they find the minimum moves, how do they know its even minimal.

Now after being in a CS major for over 3 years, I finally understand these systems fairly. So I decided to make a klotski solver.

I wanted to make it fun so I stored the whole game board in an integer (uint64_t), as I like integers more than vectors. And then I got the urge to minify the engine to the max extent I could, so shrunk it down to 311 bytes from ~3.5 KB. The engine is only the searching part though.

The solver is a BFS that explores every reachable position. For the classic start it finds the best solution in 116 moves, after exploring all 25,955 reachable states in about 2-4 ms.

Here's the repo; any feedback is welcomed : ) https://github.com/Dream-World-Coder/depuzzled

records.title: Show HN: I built a directory to set up ChatGPT's always-on agents in one paste
records.author: iamdemetrius
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Demetrius.

When OpenAI launched Dots (always-on agents in ChatGPT that run in the background, connect to your apps, and ask before risky actions), I wanted to set one up and went looking for examples of what other people were telling theirs. I couldn't find any.

Each Dot comes down to three things: its instructions, the apps it can reach, and Custom Rules (Allow / Require approval / Block). The rules matter most, because they decide what the agent does without asking you. They're also the part nobody was sharing.

So I built DotBotDirectory.

Each entry has the Dot's job, its instructions, its connected apps, and its three rule lists. One click copies the instructions and rules together so you can paste them into your own Dot.

Where it stands:

- 26 starter entries, written by me from ideas people published in early Dot write-ups. Each one credits its source.

- None of them have been tested on a real Dot yet, and they're labelled "Starter - untested". I'll mark entries as tested once someone confirms one works.

- Copy counts start at zero, so nothing looks more popular than it is.

- Free, and not affiliated with OpenAI.

Two questions for anyone who has run a Dot:

1. What did you put in Require approval vs Block? That's where I think most of the value is.

2. Did your Dot ever do something you didn't expect? I'd like to turn those cases into rules other people can copy.

Happy to answer anything.

records.author: hyperb1iss
records.storyText:
Light it up with Hypercolor, a new RGB lighting orchestration platform for all platforms and all devices. Effects are web pages (or glsl), rendered by an internal browser GPU accelerated all the way to the pixels. It's pure rust from the Servo renderer to the WASM UI.

Comes with 40+ effects, supports ambilight, display faces, system monitoring, screen casting, and audio. Device support is pretty good but it's early and this is where we need the most help! You can find the full support matrix on the site, and there is also an OpenRGB bridge as a fallback. There's support for a few unique devices too like the Ableton Push 2 and ROLI Blocks. My favorite thing about this engine is the ability to create multiple effect zones and manage them independently! My whole house runs on it now. It's Apache licensed, and a cloud service is coming with remote and smart home support. A Home Assistant integration is already available.

The best way to set up Hypercolor is to just have an agent do it for you using the bundled skill. Just describe your setup, case type, hardware, etc, and it will find all the specs and configure it for you. Or just do it the good old-fashioned way in Studio!

Please check it out and file and issue if you're looking for device support. I can only build drivers for devices I have access too, please open PRs if you're able to contribute! Agents can reverse engineer your hardware and build a driver easily, if you want to go that route (the repo is designed for agents). We have a full TypeScript effects SDK for easy effect creation too, and support existing Lightscript based html effects out of the box.

I've had a lot of fun building this and I hope you enjoy it!
